https://www.politico.eu/article/spain-an.text: Thousands of Spanish and Moroccan security officers reinforced Ceuta’s borders on Friday as online messages spread calling for a new mass incursion into the exclave in North Africa. Following last month’s unprecedented arrival of 72,000 migrants into the Spanish city, viral social media posts proposed a similar surge be staged on Saturday, Aug. 15 — a national holiday in Spain. Authorities in Madrid and Rabat have been tracking the online chatter and coordinating a common response. Moroccan Interior Ministry Spokesperson Rachid El Khalfi on Wednesday confirmed the country was “taking all necessary measures to counter any attempt at illegal crossing,” and local journalists reported a significant buildup of troops around the border town of Fnideq on Friday. Advertisement Advertisement Spanish Interior Minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska traveled to Ceuta on Thursday to inspect border infrastructure and a new sea barrier designed to keep people from swimming into the city. The exclave’s security personnel has also been reinforced with an additional 300 police officers and 2,000 soldiers. “We do this to dissuade anyone who aspires to enter Ceuta and Melilla irregularly,” said Grande-Marlaska. “None of them will remain in Ceuta, none of them will make it to the Iberian Peninsula, none of them will be given legal status.” The rumored mass crossing has been cited by critics of Spain’s migration policies. Austria’s conservative Europe, Integration and Family Minister Claudia Bauer, last week mentioned the rumored Aug. 15 surge in a written statement, demanding Madrid “immediately and significantly reinforce border protection in its African enclaves and ensure that this time it will hold.” Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni’s government also cited the possibility of a mid-August mass arrival last week while justifying its decision to maintain border checks on travelers from Spain.

Photograph: Vyacheslav Prokofyev/Pool Sputnik Kremlin/AP Russia Putin consolidates grip on Russia as 49 Ukraine war veterans elected to parliament United Russia party’s record victory in tightly controlled vote likely to be used as evidence of support for war against Ukraine Luke Harding and agencies Mon 21 Sep 2026 09.40 EDT Last modified on Mon 21 Sep 2026 12.53 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Russia’s new parliament will include 49 deputies who have taken part in the war against Ukraine , officials have said after a landslide victory by the ruling United Russia party in widely criticised elections. The pro-Kremlin party won a record 355 seats in the country’s 450-seat Duma lower house of parliament, according to preliminary figures. The result further consolidates Vladimir Putin’s grip on power and gives United Russia a super-majority bigger than its previous 2016 record of 343 seats. The polls are the first to be held since Putin’s 2022 full-scale invasion . United Russia’s general secretary, Vladimir Yakushev, said 86 veterans from Moscow’s “special military operation” were likely to have been elected. “This is quite a substantial contribution,” he said. He later revised the number to 49. View image in fullscreen As Russia counted the votes from its widely criticised election, Kremlin forces attacked targets in Ukraine, damaging the historic Zaporizhzhia National University. Photograph: Ukrinform/Shutterstock Putin’s press spokesperson, Dmitry Peskov, said the vote showed that Russians supported their longtime leader, who has ruled as prime minister or president since 2000 . “These indicators, of course, point to the highest level of consolidation within Russian society around the head of state,” Peskov said. Western governments denounced the polls held in Russian-occupied areas of Ukraine as a “sham”. Russia’s supreme court last month banned the only party that opposes the war, Yabloko, from participating, leaving liberal voters with no option to express discontent. Kaja Kallas, the EU’s top diplomat, called the election “another major setback for Russian democracy”. “The Kremlin silenced dissent and shut out international election monitors,” Kallas wrote on X, adding: “The veneer of democracy is all that remains.” The elections come amid speculation that Putin may announce a large mobilisation campaign this autumn, in an attempt to inject fresh momentum to Russia’s bogged down military campaign. Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has suggested the Kremlin wants to recruit another 300,000 troops. View image in fullscreen Aftermath of a Russian drone attack in Zaporizhzhia. Photograph: Reuters In recent months, Russia has escalated its bombardment, pummelling Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities with jet-powered attack drones. Ukraine has launched its own deep strikes, hitting Moscow’s oil refinery on Sunday , as part of what Zelenskyy has dubbed “long-range sanctions”. Russia’s has also intensified its campaign to seize a string of cities in Ukraine’s eastern Donbas region, including Kramatorsk and Sloviansk. So far, it has been unable to break through, with Ukrainian commanders reporting their own counteroffensive near the city of Lyman. Inside Russia, criticism of the conflict is banned. Anti-war bloggers have been arrested and jailed . A local politician, Boris Nadezhdin, who previously tried to stand in presidential elections on a peace ticket, was barred from September’s elections and accused of being a “foreign agent”. The other parties that won seats in this month’s poll all support the “special military operation”. They include the communists, who came second with 40 seats, the ultra-nationalist LDPR party, with 25, and the New People party, with 20. Chechnya’s leader, Ramzan Kadyrov, a Putin ally, was re-elected and said to have won more than 99% of the votes. View image in fullscreen A shopping centre, struck during Russia’s drone attack on in Zaporizhzhia. Photograph: Reuters/Stringer Russia’s elections chief, Ella Pamfilova, said United Russia had won a resounding victory with 57.83%, with 95% of ballots counted, up from the 49.8% it won in the last parliamentary election, in 2021. She praised voters for resisting “psychological pressure”. Overnight, Russia carried out what Zelenskyy called a “brutal, targeted attack” on the southern city of Zaporizhzhia. He said a nine-storey residential building, a university building, a shopping centre, and a boiler house were all damaged, with five people injured. A woman in Kharkiv region was killed in a drone strike. Zelenskyy said: “Russia is not scaling back its escalatory actions and is signalling a readiness to expand the war. All this is happening against the backdrop of global stability already having been shattered by this war. We must continue to pressure the aggressor to bring this war to an end.” Explore more on these topics Russia Vladimir Putin Europe Ukraine Volodymyr Zelenskyy news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story Ukraine targets Moscow with hundreds of drones on final day of Russian election ‘The rules have changed’: has Russia begun to order assassinations on US soil? Bos , Worthy News Europe Bureau Chief KYIV/MOSCOW/BUDAPEST ( Worthy News ) – Russia is leaving the door open to new peace talks with Ukraine following a weekend of intense American diplomacy, but major obstacles remain to ending the war, now in its fifth year. https://www.worthynews.com/wordpressimages/2026/09/WorthyNewsRadioSep7.mp3 Moscow said Monday it does not rule out renewed peace talks involving Russia, Ukraine, and the United States. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov spoke after U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv. Start your day with Christian news and biblical encouragement from Worthy News. “We also do not rule out the resumption of this trilateral format, but it is premature to talk about the venue and the exact timing at this stage,” Peskov said through an interpreter. “Of course, any efforts that are more or less effective are one small step towards peace,” he added. ENVOYS ARRIVE BY TRAIN Following their talks in Moscow, Kushner and Witkoff traveled to Kyiv by train from Poland, with Zelenskyy saying Russian strikes had prevented them from flying into the Ukrainian capital. Russia and Ukraine had agreed to refrain from striking each other’s capitals during the American delegation’s visits. Zelenskyy joked that the presence of the two U.S. envoys had done even more than Patriot air defenses to protect Kyiv, urging them to come more often so its residents could “live a little.” The Kremlin described Saturday’s talks with Putin as “highly useful,” while the Americans called their subsequent discussions with Zelenskyy “encouraging.” Neither meeting produced a breakthrough. TERRITORY REMAINS OBSTACLE One of the biggest obstacles remains territory. Putin insists Russia intends to take the remaining Ukrainian-held areas of the eastern Donetsk region. Zelenskyy says Ukraine cannot reward Russia for its invasion by simply surrendering territory and says such questions ultimately need to be discussed by the countries’ leaders. Security guarantees for Ukraine are another sticking point. WINTER SUPPORT DISCUSSED In Kyiv, Zelenskyy discussed air defenses, including additional Patriot systems, and what he called a “winter package” of American and European support for Ukraine’s energy infrastructure. He acknowledged that the fighting now appeared likely to continue into another winter. The U.S. envoys nevertheless sounded cautiously optimistic. Witkoff said both Russia and Ukraine would have to compromise but added that Washington believes it has the “ingredients” needed to move toward an agreement. Kushner said the weekend mission had produced new ideas for advancing the negotiations. MORE TALKS EXPECTED The Americans are now hoping another round of U.S.-mediated Russian-Ukrainian talks can be announced soon. Ukraine, the United States and European representatives have also agreed to hold another meeting, although its location has not yet been decided. Yet fighting continues despite the diplomatic push. Russian-appointed authorities in occupied Crimea said a Ukrainian drone attack on Sevastopol killed two people, including a teenage girl, while Ukraine said it struck Russia’s Ryazan oil refinery hundreds of kilometers inside Russian territory. CLASHES CONTINUE Moscow also said its forces struck a Ukrainian cargo vessel in the Black Sea that it claimed was carrying Western-supplied military equipment. The clashes underscored that despite renewed diplomatic momentum, the fundamental question remains unresolved: whether Moscow and Kyiv are prepared to make the compromises Washington says will be necessary to end Europe’s bloodiest conflict in generations. Photograph: Olivier Chassignole/AFP/Getty Images France ‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policing Unprecedented protests that began in low-income banlieue are turning ugly, with investigations under way into police brutality Angelique Chrisafis in Paris Tue 6 Oct 2026 07.28 EDT Last modified on Tue 6 Oct 2026 08.10 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google B efore dawn on Tuesday outside the Lycée Sophie-Germain in central Paris , hundreds of teenagers dragged wheelie bins, metal barriers and shopping trolleys to build a barricade outside the front door of their secondary school. Climbing to the top of the piles of bins, pupils held banners calling for more funding and greater equality in French schools. But they were also protesting against French riot police, who have been accused by human rights groups of using disproportionate force against children in what is fast becoming the biggest youth protest movement in decades . “Everyone hates the police,” chanted a group of 15- and 16-year-olds. At least 215 teenagers, 715 police officers and 85 teaching staff have been injured in clashes in recent days, according to the government. “We’re teenagers with wheelie bins, and the police have heavy weapons, it’s totally mismatched,” said Livia, 17, who was studying theatre at a lycée in northern Paris and did not want her real name published. “The police are extremely violent in France . This is state violence and it’s horrible seeing police allowed to target children. It’s important to remember this is institutionalised violence, it’s planned and deliberate.” View image in fullscreen A large student protest in Nantes on Tuesday. Photograph: Stéphane Mahé/Reuters Ten investigations into possible police brutality are under way after injuries allegedly involving the use of police weapons, including one 15-year-old who lost his hand , another who lost his eye and a boy whose jaw and teeth were shattered, leaving him, as his mother said, barely able to eat with a straw in hospital. “The policing is catastrophic, people have been mutilated by weapons – one boy has lost an eye – it’s horrible,” said Lily, 17 (not her real name), who was studying social sciences in her final year of school and demonstrating for more funding in what she called a discriminatory education system that left poorer children behind. “My parents support me being on the barricades and at the protests. They’re worried about the policing, but they said they’d come and get me from the police station if I was arrested.” Teenagers nearby held up cardboard signs protesting against the use of teargas and riot police. “A state that gases high school students is a weak state,” read one banner. “Gas rapists, not children,” said another sign in reference to calls for betters laws against sexual violence. Another banner read: “Not here to riot.” View image in fullscreen French riot police in Lyon on Tuesday. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters The unprecedented protest movement that began outside one school in a low-income Paris suburb has spread across the country, taking the government by surprise. Hundreds of high schools have been barricaded and forced to close as pupils protest against teacher shortages, crumbling buildings and overcrowded classes. The justice ministry said 5,060 people had been arrested ⁠since the protests began, 87% of them being minors. More than 1,800 people had been prosecuted, ​including 1,483 minors, the ministry said, without specifying ​the crimes. It said 790 cases had been ​dismissed. The government said 24 schools had been burned or ransacked. “In more than 20 years of teaching, I’ve never seen protests this big,” said one teacher at Sophie-Germain high school who planned to join the Paris demonstration on Tuesday afternoon. “The students in central Paris have shown a great sense of solidarity with those in the Paris suburbs who face much worse conditions in their schools. There’s a feeling of solidarity and generosity between teenagers that flies in the face of the notion that we live in an era of selfishness. No one knows how long this will go on for.” View image in fullscreen A protester in Montpellier on Friday. Photograph: Horcajuelo Guillaume/EPA Tens of thousands of students, trade unionists and parents are expected to march in support of the protests across France on Tuesday afternoon, including in Paris, Toulouse, Nice and Bordeaux, with riot police on alert. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to This is Europe The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment after newsletter promotion Isabella, 16, said she had the backing of her parents, who work in film and music. “Young people have been teargassed for doing nothing but trying to express their opinion. Everybody told us that school was the great leveller, but today that is not the case at all. A teenager in the banlieue [suburbs] of Paris is never going to have the same opportunities as a student from the city centre. That’s why we’re here today.” Lionel, 17, who was in his final year at school and hoped to study English, said: “The aim isn’t to riot or smash things up, we just want to protest peacefully.” View image in fullscreen Demonstrations in Paris on Tuesday. Photograph: Tom Nicholson/Reuters Teenagers also chanted songs against Marine Le Pen , the far-right, anti-immigration candidate in the 2027 presidential election, who is high in the polls as Emmanuel Macron steps down after a decade in office. Many teenagers were worried about the election. “We’re also protesting against the growth of the far right,” said Aislinn. Justine, 17, who had been at the barricade since before dawn, said she hoped the protest would continue and grow into a “massive” movement. “For years, there has been a mental health crisis among young people in France and anger at rundown schools and the stresses of the education system. We need the government to listen to us and make radical change.” View image in fullscreen Protests in Lyon on Tuesday. Photograph: Denis Balibouse/Reuters Students’ names have been changed. https://telex.hu/belfold/2026/10/23/magy.text: Menü Kereső Ránk számíthattok! 3000 új támogatót keresünk Csatlakozom Magyar Péter: Aki egy agresszort menteget, semmit sem ért '56 üzenetéből Belföld Fotó: Huszti István / Telex Mizsur András Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom „Aki egy agresszort menteget, vagy idegen birodalmaknak rendelné alá a nemzetet, az semmit sem ért 1956 üzenetéből, legyen az Budapesten vagy egy párizsi teraszon” – mondta Magyar Péter miniszterelnök a Kossuth téren megtartott 1956-os állami ünnepségen. Ezzel Orbán Viktorra utalt, akit egy párizsi szálloda előtt fotóztak le , miközben Budapesten az október 23-i megemlékezések zajlottak. Magyar szerint 1956 hősei azt is örökül hagyták a magyar vezetőknek, hogy a hatalmuk nem lehet fontosabb az országuk szabadságánál. Aki a saját népével szemben Moszkvában vagy bárhol máshol keres támaszt, annak legyen 1956 intő jel, hogy idegen támogatással egy ideig meg lehet tartani a hatalmat, de a magyarok szabadságvágyát nem lehet megtörni, fogalmazott. „1956 véráldozatát egyetlen magyar vezető sem teheti zárójelbe pillanatnyi gazdasági alkukért vagy kétes szövetségekért” – mondta, majd itt következett az előbb már idézett utalás Orbánra. Magyar Péter azzal kezdte a majd egyórás ünnepi beszédét, hogy köszöntötte a szabad, demokratikus, erős és „immár tényleg független Magyarországot”, és megköszönte az '56-os hősök bátorságát. Hetven éve összekapaszkodva vonultak az egyetemisták, a gyári munkások, pesti lányok és srácok. Hisz benne, hogy akkor sem cserélték volna el a sorsukat, ha tudták volna, hogy mi vár rájuk. „Nincs megrendítőbb és felemelőbb dolog annál, hogy pontosan 70 évvel később ugyanezen a téren állhatunk szabadon.” Azt mondta, volt tizenhárom dicsőséges nap, amikor a magyarok egységesen kiáltották, hogy ruszkik, haza! Magyar a forradalom leveréséről szólva azt mondta, hogy a katonai túlerő leverhette a forradalmat, kivégezhették Nagy Imrét és a hősöket, de azt a felismerést, hogy képesek a kezükbe venni a sorsunkat, többé nem vehették el a magyaroktól. A magyar forradalom után tisztességes ember többé nem mondhatta azt, hogy a kommunizmus a szabadságot és a népet szolgálja. A forradalom után a hatalom nem érte be puszta bosszúval, azt akarták, hogy a magyar gyanakodjon a magyarra – mondta Magyar Péter, szerinte ennek vált véres szimbólumává Nagy Imre, Maléter Pál és Gyimes Miklós kivégzése. „Látjuk őket magunk előtt, ahogy hajnal 5 órakor kilépnek zárkájukból, látjuk a három fagerendát, halljuk az elhadart ítéletet.” Szerinte Nagy Imre, Maléter Pál és Gyimes Miklós a független és demokratikus Magyarországért adta életét. „Ezt a hazát soha többé nem hagyjuk eltiporni.” Felidézte, hogy a forradalom után magyarok ezrei voltak kénytelenek útnak indulni, és a nagyszülei is köztük voltak. „A nagymamám döntésének köszönhető, hogy itt állok önök előtt” – mondta Magyar, felidézve, mit mondott a nagyanyja a nagyapjának, mielőtt elindultak volna: „Palkó, kedves, én nem tudok elmenni.” Magyar Péter megköszönte minden nemzetnek, hogy befogadták a hazájukból elmenekülő magyarokat. A miniszterelnök szerint '56 minden nemzedéknek tartogat valamit, majd a március 15-i beszédére utalt vissza, szerinte nem volt hiábavaló a harc és az áldozat, mert ma Magyarország erős és demokratikus. Szerinte ’56-ban azt is követelték, hogy legyen becsülete a munkának, hogy a magyar ember szabadnak érezhesse magát a hazájában. Ezt az örökséget viszik tovább, olyan országot építenek, ahol a szabadság mellé tisztes megélhetés és megbecsültség is jár. Nem érti a forradalmat az, aki méricskéli, kiknek jár a hálánk, mondta Magyar – majd az egy évvel ezelőtti október 23-i beszédét idézte fel. „Arról álmodtunk akkor, hogy egy szabad, működő országban ünnepelhetjük október 23-át. Ezt akarnák a hőseink is.” Arról is beszélt, hogy „hosszú éveken át azt hazudták nekünk, hogy a nemzeti ünnep csak egy politikai oldalnak jár, de ennek vége”. Ezután azzal folytatta, hogy most rajtuk a sor, hogy tegyenek a szabadságért. Magyarország nem lehet kompország, nem sodródhat kelet és nyugat között – jelentette ki. 1956-ban is a szabad, demokratikus Európát választották a magyarok. Magyar úgy fogalmazott: különutak helyett megbízható szövetségesek akarunk lenni, akik emelt fővel ülnek az asztalnál, és okos, a jövőbe tekintő nemzetté akarunk válni. A győzelem nem cél, csupán eszköz, emlékeztetett a miniszterelnök. Azt ígérte, hogy a megszerzett hatalmat soha nem használják fel saját népük ellen, a törvény újra egyformán érvényes lesz mindenkire, nem gyártanak új ellenségeket. „A szabadság több annál, mint hogy nem kell egy másik nemzet alá hajtanunk a fejünket. Hogy a kórházban hagyott csecsemők, a bántalmazott nők védelmet kapjanak, hogy az állam intézményei értünk dolgozzanak, és a vitáinkat érvekkel döntsük el” – sorolta Magyar a teendőket, és azt kérte, kapaszkodjanak össze a magyarok. Szerinte jó lenne olyan országot hagyni a gyerekeinkre, amire büszkék lehetünk. „Ez itt a mi hazánk, és mi bármire képesek vagyunk érte” – mondta Magyar, majd azzal zárta beszédét, hogy éljen a magyar szabadság, gloria victis.
